To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) for PAC learning of Boolean functions, a simple baseline algorithm achieves optimal sample complexity, (2) for learning of thresholds on a real line, a simple baseline achieves optimal sample complexity without any overhead, (3) for a number of convex regression problems, we achieve a significant improvement in sample complexity over existing approaches, and (4) we establish strong generalization guarantees for all private algorithms

(1) the overhead of private aggregation can be avoided for a number of natural settings of convex regression, and (2) for learning Boolean functions, private aggregation can be used to achieve optimal sample complexity.

(i) it is possible to achieve differential privacy of individual predictions with nearly optimal sample complexity, (ii) the overhead of the private prediction problem is significant for many standard settings, and (iii) this overhead can be eliminated for a number of natural classes of functions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how much data is required to ensure differential privacy in the prediction setting.
the question of whether it is possible to learn a private model without incurring a substantial overhead, and we show that in some settings the answer is yes.
the fundamental question of how much data is necessary to learn a private predictor, as opposed to a private model, and how to efficiently achieve this goal.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
for many learning problems it is possible to ensure differential privacy of predictions at a small cost.
the privacy-preserving prediction is a hard problem, but there are some settings where it can be made efficient.

the overhead of privacy is negligible for some problems (e.g., convex regression, learning a threshold on a line, or PAC learning of any concept class) and significant for others (e.g. learning of a threshold on a hyperplane or a non-convex function).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
for many learning problems, differential privacy of individual predictions can be achieved at nearly optimal sample complexity, and with a small overhead.

we show that the overhead of ensuring differential privacy of individual predictions can be avoided for a number of basic learning problems, and that the sample complexity of private prediction is nearly-optimal for realizable learning.
, for some problems, we can achieve the same accuracy as non-private algorithms with a small overhead.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in some applications the overheads associated with ensuring differential privacy of predictions may be significantly reduced compared to the cost of ensuring privacy of the model itself.
in some settings, privacy-preserving prediction can be much more efficient than privacy-preserving model training.
the overhead of privacy can be avoided if the prediction algorithm is designed carefully.
